title: Minutes Battles to Watch
brief: Which players are in a fight for minutes or a starting job, and which battles matter for our auction prices? It must note the hedge option of buying both candidates cheaply and cutting the loser, and that a starting job alone does not guarantee minutes.
summary: Minutes battles lower auction prices, so they are where our league finds value, but only when you have a reason to expect your player wins the job. For battles you cannot call, buy both candidates for 1 to 2 USD late in the auction and cut the loser once minutes are clear. Judge every battle by minutes per game, not by who is announced as the starter, because a bench player can play as many minutes as a starter.

paragraphs.text: When some drafters think a player might lose his starting job or share minutes, his price drops. If you believe he will start, that drop is value for you. In our auction on 2026-10-18, look for these discounts among mid-priced players. Bid toward his full-role value only when the experts expect him to win the battle.

Small losses still count. Losing even two to three minutes a game limits a player's upside and lowers his draft value. If a battle is truly open, take a few dollars off your top bid rather than paying for a full role. A player who loses part of his minutes is a weaker pick, even if he never loses the starting label.

sections.heading: A starting job does not guarantee minutes

paragraphs.text: A starting spot can matter less than minutes. A bench player can play about as many minutes as a nominal starter. So do not pay extra just because a player is named the starter in preseason, and do not drop a sixth man just because he comes off the bench. What decides his value for us is his minutes per game and whether he closes games.

Concrete rule: for every battle player you roster, write down the minutes he needs. The player lines below give those numbers, often 25 to 30 minutes. In the first two weeks of the season, compare his real minutes with that number. Do not rely on the box score label of starter or bench.

sections.heading: Crowded rosters: project the rotation first

paragraphs.text: Coaches do not play 12 or more players. When a team is overstocked at one position, some good players will lose playing time, and some will get no real minutes unless injuries open them up.

When a team has too many players at the same positions, the minutes get spread thin and fewer of them are draftable. Before you reach for anyone on a crowded team, project the rotation. In our 144-player draft, that usually means buying the one or two players you expect to keep the role. Leave the rest on waivers. When an injury opens minutes, add them with FAB. Remember the limit of 6 acquisitions per week.

sections.heading: The hedge: buy both, cut the loser

paragraphs.text: Two experts give the same late-draft hedge. Draft both candidates in a battle for a starting job or the same minutes. See which one wins the role. Then drop the other.

In our league, use the hedge only at the end of the auction, when both players cost 1 to 2 USD. We have only 2 bench spots, so one hedge pair takes up most of your bench. Do not hedge if one candidate costs real money, because then you pay twice for one role. Cut the loser as soon as his minutes fall clearly below the number he needs. Use the open spot for a FAB pickup. Daily waivers make the swap quick.

sections.heading: Where the notes pull in different directions

paragraphs.text: The notes do not disagree outright, but they push in different directions. One side says a minutes battle creates value: the price drops, you buy the player you expect to start, or you hedge both. The other side warns that crowded rosters spread minutes thin, that some good players simply lose time, and that losing even two to three minutes lowers a player's value. Here is how to use both. Buy the discount only when the experts expect your player to win. Otherwise, wait until the 1 to 2 USD stage and hedge, or leave the battle to waivers.

Before the auction on 2026-10-18, check the final preseason starting lineups and injury news for every battle you plan to bid on. In the first two weeks of the season, check three things: minutes per game against each player's target, who closes games, and injuries to the players ahead of him. If a player loses two to three minutes from his projected role, lower your view of him. If a bench player gets starter-level minutes, treat him as a starter.
